title: SnapJoy
subtitle: A folding phone gimbal with an inflatable lower grip
role: Research, concept, grip testing, CMF and model making
summary: SnapJoy is a folding phone gimbal with an inflatable lower grip that collapses into the palm. Watching how people lived in 2023 in the time of social media, I kept asking what they actually needed when filming. With phone cameras getting better every year, I wondered why anyone still carried an action camera or a pocket camera, and whether one simple tool could let the phone be enough.

sections.heading: Could the phone be enough
sections.body:
Shooting, editing and uploading already happen on a single phone. Mapping daily, travel and study vlogs on a wall showed people switching shooting postures constantly, flipping repeatedly between front and rear cameras, and pausing video to take still photographs. Card-based interviews comparing shots already in people's phone albums against the vlogs they imagined making showed a wish to document daily life in a richer form.

Mapping existing phone accessories showed why that stays awkward. Selfie sticks are slow to mount, gimbals get in the way of stills, rigs are cumbersome to assemble, and camera-style grips fall short for video and selfies. Each tool only answered part of the job.

sections.heading: Folding several jobs into one
sections.body:
Thinking about how the magnetic attachment on the back of a phone lets it turn to another angle led me to ask whether a portable stabiliser could also take different angles, directions and roles. I wanted one object that could be held like a camera for photographs, unfold as a gimbal for video, and turn around for selfies, while staying as simple to use as possible.

Finding that structure took many tries. I analysed gimbal motor layouts, built a cardboard arm to test a secondary folding structure, and shaped clay blocks to find where a camera-style shutter should sit under the finger. Sketching along ergonomics and novelty tracks brought up an inflatable PVC airbag handle that pulls out and inflates for shooting, then folds back to keep the stowed volume small.

sections.heading: Grips, internals and the model
sections.body:
I built four hand models to test different inflatable grips. A camera-like shutter felt familiar and mixing hard and soft surfaces improved comfort, though one tester did not want the primary holding zone to be soft and people expected shortcut keys. Scoring the two workable directions favoured the more compact, storable option. I refined that grip through nine small grey models, then took apart an existing gimbal to verify that its mainboard, motor drive, operator panel and shutter button fit inside the new shell, with the battery in the lower telescopic section.

The finished gimbal combines a press-and-hold unlock button for switching modes with a flash, shutter, selfie fill LED and filter switching across four milky-white colourways paired with low-saturation accents. I built a physical model in the green colourway from small parts and translucent green grip pieces to judge it both folded in the palm and extended in the hand.
